sections.title: Placement of Subsurface Drainage System
sections.summary: See 20-3.5.1 through 20-3.5.3 for rigid-pavement, flexible-pavement, and separation-layer placement guidance.
sections.body: See the subsections below for placement rules by pavement type and for the separation layer.
key_points: See 20-3.5.1 through 20-3.5.3 for rigid-pavement, flexible-pavement, and separation-layer placement guidance.
sections.applicability: Overview of drainage-layer placement rules.

sections.title: Rigid Pavements (Placement)
sections.summary: Drainage layer (plus any granular separation layer) goes directly beneath the slab and counts as a structural base layer.
sections.body: In the case of rigid pavements the drainage layer, if required, must be placed directly beneath the concrete slab. In the structural design of the concrete slab the drainage layer along with any granular separation layer must be considered a base layer, and structural benefit may be realized from the layers.
key_points: Drainage layer (plus any granular separation layer) goes directly beneath the slab and counts as a structural base layer.
sections.applicability: Drainage layer placement in rigid pavement sections.

sections.title: Flexible Pavements (Placement)
sections.summary: Place beneath the graded-crushed-aggregate base if subbase thickness >= drainage+separation layer thickness; if total structure <12 in, may place directly beneath the surface layer (used as the base itself); limit aggregate base above the drainage layer to <=8% passing No. 200.
sections.body: In the case of flexible pavements the drainage layer should be placed either directly beneath the surface layer or beneath a graded crushed aggregate base course. If the required thickness of granular subbase is equal to or greater than the thickness of the drainage layer plus the thickness of the separation layer, the drainage layer is placed beneath the graded crushed aggregate base. Where the total thickness of pavement structure is less than 12 in (300 mm), the drainage layer may be placed directly beneath the surface layer and the drainage layer used as a base. When the drainage layer is placed beneath an unbound aggregate base, care must be taken to limit the material passing the No. 200 (0.08 mm) sieve in the aggregate base to 8 percent or less.
key_points: 12-in (300 mm) total structure threshold decides whether the drainage layer sits directly under the surface (acting as base) or under a separate aggregate base.
sections.applicability: Drainage layer placement in flexible pavement sections.

sections.title: Separation Layer (Placement)
sections.summary: Separation layer sits directly beneath the drainage layer (typically a 50-CBR-subbase-grade graded aggregate, countable as subbase); filter fabric may substitute where a firm foundation already exists and thickness isn't needed for subgrade protection; frost areas need an NFS separation layer.
sections.body: The drainage layer must be protected from contamination of fines from the underlying layers by a separation layer to be placed directly beneath the drainage layer. In most cases the separation layer should be a graded aggregate material meeting the requirements of a 50 CBR subbase and can be considered as part of the subbase. For design situations where a firm foundation already exists and thickness of the separation layer is not needed in the structure for protection of the subgrade, a filter fabric may be substituted for the granular separation layer. In frost areas the separation layer should be NFS.
key_points: Separation layer sits directly beneath the drainage layer (typically a 50-CBR-subbase-grade graded aggregate, countable as subbase); filter fabric may substitute where a firm foundation already exists and thickness isn't needed for subgrade protection; frost areas need an NFS...
sections.applicability: Separation layer placement and material selection.

sections.title: Material Properties for Drainage Layers
sections.summary: Drainage material: hard/durable crushed aggregate, well-graded enough for construction stability while retaining permeability; two grades -- RDM (1,000-5,000 ft/day, structurally usable as base/subbase) and OGM (>5,000 ft/day, usually needs stabilization for construction/structural use); Table 20-3 gradation limits, Table 20-4 design properties, Table 20-5 gives 3 stable gradations (max sizes 3/4, 1, 1-1/2 in) each achieving ~1,000 ft/day.
sections.body: The material for a drainage layer should be a hard, durable crushed aggregate to withstand degradation under construction traffic as well as in service traffic. The gradation of the material should be such that the material has sufficient stability for the operation of construction equipment. While it is desirable for strength and stability to have the well-graded aggregate, the permeability of the material must be maintained. For most drainage layers, the drainage materials should have a minimum permeability of 1,000 ft/day (300 m/day). Two materials, a rapid draining material (RDM) and an open graded material (OGM), have been identified for use in drainage layers. The RDM is a material having a sufficiently high permeability (1,000 ft/day to 5,000 ft/day (1,500 m/day)) to serve as a drainage layer and will also have the stability to support construction equipment and the structural strength to serve as a base or a subbase. The OGM is a material having a very high permeability (greater than 5,000 ft/day) which can be used for a drainage layer. The OGM will normally require stabilization for construction stability and for structural strength to serve as a base in a flexible pavement. Gradation limits for the two materials are given in Table 20-3 and the design properties are given in Table 20-4. The gradations given in Table 20-3 provide very wide bands and it is possible to produce gradations within these bands that may not be sufficiently stable for construction without the use of chemical stabilization. Table 20-5 provides the gradation specifications for three aggregate materials each of which will meet the criteria for stability. These gradations were developed to produce the maximum density given maximum aggregate sizes of 1-1/2 in (38 mm), 1 in (25mm), and 3/4 in (19mm) and a maximum of 8 percent passing the number 16 sieve. For drainage layer thicknesses less than 6 in (150 mm), gradations number 1 or 2 may be used. For drainage layers 6 in. or more in thickness any of the three gradations may be used but the gradations having the larger size aggregates will produce the more stable aggregate. Each of the gradations would produce a drainage layer having a permeability of about 1000 ft/day.
key_points: RDM (1,000-5,000 ft/day): stable enough for construction AND structural base/subbase use without stabilization.
OGM (>5,000 ft/day): usually needs stabilization for construction/structural use.
Drainage layer < 6 in: use Table 20-5 gradation No. 1 or 2 only; >= 6 in: any of the three.

sections.title: Aggregate for Separation Layer
sections.summary: Separation-layer aggregate meets 50-CBR-subbase requirements (Table 6-1) except max aggregate size <= 1/4 the layer thickness; must be more permeable than the subgrade but not so open it allows pumping (D15/D85 ratio <= 5 vs. subgrade); Table 20-6 gives full material property requirements.
sections.body: The separation layer prevents fines from infiltrating or pumping into the drainage layer and provides a working platform for construction and compaction of the drainage layer. The material for the separation layer should be a graded aggregate meeting the requirements of a 50 CBR subbase as given in Chapter titled Flexible Pavement Select Materials and Subbase Courses except that the maximum aggregate size should not be greater than 1/4 the thickness of the separation layer. The permeability of the separation layer should be greater than the permeability of the subgrade, but the material should not be so open as to permit pumping of fines into the separation layer. To prevent pumping of fines the ratio of d15 of the separation layer to d85 of the subgrade must be equal to or less than 5. The material property requirements for the separation layer are given in Table 20-6.
key_points: Separation layer piping check: D15(separation layer) / D85(subgrade) <= 5.

sections.title: Filter Fabric for Separation Layer
sections.summary: Filter fabric protects against pumping but adds no compaction-support stability -- use only where the subgrade already supports drainage-layer compaction; must be nonwoven needle-punched, meeting Table 20-7 strength/AOS criteria.
sections.body: Although filter fabric provides protection against pumping, it does not provide extra stability for compaction of the drainage layer. Therefore, fabric should be selected only when the subgrade provides adequate support for compaction of the drainage layer. The important characteristics of the fabric are strength for surviving construction and traffic loads, and AOS to prevent pumping of fines into the drainage layer. Filter fabric for separation must be a nonwoven needle punched fabric meeting the criteria given in Table 20-7.
key_points: Filter fabric protects against pumping but adds no compaction-support stability -- use only where the subgrade already supports drainage-layer compaction; must be nonwoven needle-punched, meeting Table 20-7 strength/AOS criteria.

sections.title: Stabilization of Drainage Layer
sections.summary: OGM usually needs stabilization for stability/strength/handling durability; may also apply to RDM or when high-quality crushed aggregate isn't available; methods: choke stone (mechanical) or asphalt/Portland cement binder (chemical).
sections.body: Stabilization of OGM is normally required for stability and strength, and to prevent degradation of the aggregate in handling and compaction. Stabilization may also be used when high quality crushed aggregate is not available and there may even be occasions when stabilization of RDM is necessary. Stabilization may be accomplished mechanically by use of a choke stone or by the use of a binder such as asphalt or Portland cement.
key_points: OGM usually needs stabilization for stability/strength/handling durability; may also apply to RDM or when high-quality crushed aggregate isn't available; methods: choke stone (mechanical) or asphalt/Portland cement binder (chemical).
sections.applicability: Overview of drainage-layer stabilization options.

sections.title: Choke Stone Stabilization
sections.summary: Choke stone: small hard/durable crushed aggregate (90% fractured faces) stabilizing an OGM surface; D15(coarse)/D15(choke) < 5 and D50(coarse)/D50(choke) > 2; gradation range per Table 20-3.
sections.body: A choke stone is a small size stone used to stabilize the surface of an OGM. The choke stone should be a hard, durable, crushed aggregate having 90 percent fractured faces. The ratio of d15 of the coarse aggregate to the d15 of the choke stone must be less than 5, and the ratio of the d50 of the coarse aggregate to d50 of the choke stone must be greater than 2. The gradation range for acceptable choke stone is given in Table 20-3.
key_points: Choke stone gradation ratios: D15(coarse)/D15(choke) < 5; D50(coarse)/D50(choke) > 2.
tables: Table 20-3: Gradations of Materials for Drainage Layers and Choke Stone
sections.applicability: Mechanical (choke stone) stabilization of an OGM drainage layer.

sections.title: Asphalt Stabilization
sections.summary: Use just enough AC20+ asphalt to coat the aggregate (not fill voids); OGM typically needs 2-2.5% by weight; less-open material (e.g. RDM) may need more.
sections.body: Stabilize the drainage material with asphalt by using only enough asphalt to coat the aggregate. Take care to not fill the voids with excess asphalt. Asphalt grade used for stabilization should be AC20 or higher. For stabilization of OGM, 2 to 2-1/2 percent asphalt by weight should be sufficient to coat the aggregate. Higher rates of application may be necessary when stabilization of less open aggregate such as RDM is necessary.
key_points: OGM asphalt stabilization: 2-2.5% by weight, AC20+ grade, coat-only (don't fill voids).
sections.applicability: Asphalt (chemical) stabilization of a drainage layer.

sections.title: Cement Stabilization
sections.summary: Use just enough Portland cement paste to coat the aggregate (not fill voids), ~2 bags/yd3 (170 kg/m3) depending on gradation; water-cement ratio just sufficient for adequate coating.
sections.body: As with asphalt stabilization, Portland cement stabilization should only use enough cement paste to coat the aggregate, and take care to not fill the voids with excess paste. The amount of Portland cement required should be about 2 bags/yd3 (170 kilograms per cubic meter) depending on the gradation of the aggregate. The water-cement ratio should be just sufficient to provide a paste which will adequately coat the aggregate.
key_points: Cement stabilization: ~2 bags/yd3 (170 kg/m3), coat-only, minimal water-cement ratio.
sections.applicability: Cement (chemical) stabilization of a drainage layer.

sections.title: Collector Drains
sections.summary: See 20-5.1 through 20-5.6 for design flow, layout, pipe material/size, backfill, geotextiles, trench cap, lateral outlets, and manholes.
sections.body: This section covers collector drain design flow, layout, pipe selection/sizing, and appurtenances (backfill, geotextiles, outlets, manholes).
key_points: See 20-5.1 through 20-5.6 for design flow, layout, pipe material/size, backfill, geotextiles, trench cap, lateral outlets, and manholes.
sections.applicability: Overview of collector drain design.

sections.title: Design Flow
sections.summary: Collector must handle drainage-layer flow (full-flowing basis) plus other sources; one-sided drainage layer: Q(mm3/s per m)=1000*H*i*k (Eq. 20-20) or Q(ft3/day per ft)=H*i*k (Eq. 20-21); double for two-sided flow.
sections.body: Provide collector drains to collect and transport water from under the pavement. For pavements having drainage layers, provide the drainage layers with a means for water to drain either with a collector or ditches. The collector system should have the capacity to handle the water from the drainage layer plus water from other sources. The water entering the collector system from the drainage layer is computed assuming the drainage layer is flowing full. Thus, the volume of water (Q) in cubic feet per day per foot (cubic millimeters per second per meter) of length of collector pipe (assuming the drainage layer is only on one side of the collector) would be: Q = 1000*H*i*k (mm3/s per m) (Equation 20-20), or Q = H*i*k (ft3/day per ft) (Equation 20-21). If the collector system has water entering from both sides, the volume of water entering the collector would be twice that given by equation 20-20.
key_points: Double the one-sided formula (Eq. 20-20/20-21) if the collector receives flow from both sides.

sections.title: Design of Collector Drains
sections.summary: See 20-5.2.1 through 20-5.2.3 for layout, pipe material, and size/slope.
sections.body: This section covers collector drain layout, pipe material selection, and pipe sizing/slope requirements.
key_points: See 20-5.2.1 through 20-5.2.3 for layout, pipe material, and size/slope.
sections.applicability: Overview of collector drain detailed design.

sections.title: Drain System Layout
sections.summary: Collectors are typically equally spaced along the shoulder (pipe, flushing/observation risers, manholes, laterals, filter fabric, backfill); avoid placing drains under the pavement when possible (settlement/heave risk), but large paved areas may require it away from high-traffic zones; cold-climate/heavy-snow areas need laterals/outlets protected from ice/snow blockage, and may need special provisions since collector pipe can stay frozen while surface thaw is occurring.
sections.body: Normally, the collector drains are equally spaced along the shoulder of the pavement. The system consists of the drain pipe, flushing and observation risers, manholes, discharge laterals, filter fabric, and trench backfill. Since placement of subsurface drains under pavements may be a source of differential settlement or heave, this should be avoided when possible. The drainage system for large areas of pavement may require placement of subsurface drains under the pavement. For these cases the subsurface drains should be placed to avoid high traffic areas. In areas of extreme cold temperatures and heavy snow buildup laterals must be placed to reduce the probability of the laterals or outlets becoming clogged with ice or snow. Also in areas of extreme cold temperatures it may not be possible to place the collector drains below the depth of frost penetration therefore it is possible that the collector pipe may be filled with ice while thawing is occurring near the surface. For this case provisions must be made to drain the upper portion of the pavement either by day-lighting the drainage layer or providing special laterals to drain the drainage layer.
key_points: Collectors are typically equally spaced along the shoulder (pipe, flushing/observation risers, manholes, laterals, filter fabric, backfill); avoid placing drains under the pavement when possible (settlement/heave risk), but large paved areas may require it away from...
sections.applicability: Collector drain system layout planning.

sections.title: Collector Pipe
sections.summary: Perforated flexible, ABS, CPE, or smooth rigid PVC; conform to AASHTO specs (CPE: M 252; PVC: M 278 Class PC 50); avoid asphalt-stabilized backfill around pipe (or use PVC EPC40/80 conduit per NEMA TC2 if unavoidable); geocomposite edge drains allowed in special cases (Government Civil Engineer approval, only where there's no drainage layer).
sections.body: The collector pipe may be perforated flexible, Acrylonitrile-Butadiene-Styrene, corrugated polyethylene (CPE) or smooth rigid polyvinyl chloride pipe (PVC). Pipe must conform to the appropriate AASHTO Specification. Most State Highway Agencies use either CPE or PVC. For CPE pipe, AASHTO specification M 252 'Corrugated Polyethylene Drainage Tubing' is suggested, while for PVC pipe, AASHTO Specification M 278, 'Class PC 50 PVC Pipe,' is recommended. It is recommended that asphalt stabilized material not be used as backfill around pipe, but, if it is to be used, then the pipe should be PVC 90 degrees C electric plastic conduct, EPC40 or EPC80 conforming to the requirements of National Electrical Manufacturers Association Specification TC2. Geocomposite edge drains (strip drains) may be used in special situations but only with the approval of the Government Civil Engineer. Geocomposite edge drains should only be considered for pavements not having a drainage layer.
key_points: Perforated flexible, ABS, CPE, or smooth rigid PVC; conform to AASHTO specs (CPE: M 252; PVC: M 278 Class PC 50); avoid asphalt-stabilized backfill around pipe (or use PVC EPC40/80 conduit per NEMA TC2 if unavoidable); geocomposite edge drains allowed in special cases...
sections.applicability: Selecting collector pipe material.

sections.title: Pipe Size and Slopes
sections.summary: Size via the Manning equation for a full-flowing circular pipe: Q(ft3/s)=(1.486/n)*A*(d/4)^(2/3)*s^(1/2) (Eq. 20-22, US) or Q(m3/s)=(1.0/n)*A*(d/4)^(2/3)*s^(1/2) (Eq. 20-23, SI); n from Table 20-8; 6-in diameter minimum for all collectors, adequate for most designs; minimum recommended subdrain slope 0.15%.
sections.body: The pipe must be sized, according to equations 20-22 or 20-23, to have a capacity sufficient to collect the peak flow from under the pavement. Equations 20-22 and 20-23 are Manning equations for computing the capacity of a full flowing circular drain. The equation for flow (Q) in cubic feet per second is: Q = (1.486/n) * A * (d/4)^(2/3) * s^(1/2) (Equation 20-22), where n = coefficient of roughness for the pipe, A = area of the pipe (ft2), d = pipe diameter (ft), s = slope of the pipe invert. For metric units the equation for flow in cubic meters per second is: Q = (1.0/n) * A * (d/4)^(2/3) * s^(1/2) (Equation 20-23), where n and s are as defined in equation 20-22, A = pipe area (m2), d = pipe diameter (m). The coefficient of roughness for different pipe types can be obtained from Table 20-8. Except for long intercepting lines and extremely severe groundwater conditions, 6 in (150 mm) diameter drains should be satisfactory for most subsurface drainage installations. The minimum size pipe recommended for all collector drains is a 6 in (150 mm) diameter pipe. The recommended minimum slope for subdrains is 0.15 percent.
key_points: Minimum collector pipe: 6 in diameter, 0.15% minimum slope.
Table 20-8 roughness: n=0.013 (clay/concrete/smooth plastic/asbestos-cement) vs. n=0.024 (corrugated metal).

sections.title: Placement of the Drainage Layer and Collector Drains
sections.summary: See 20-5.3.1 through 20-5.3.4 for design/geometry, backfill, geotextiles, and trench cap.
sections.body: This section covers collector-drain trench geometry, backfill, geotextile use, and trench cap requirements.
key_points: See 20-5.3.1 through 20-5.3.4 for design/geometry, backfill, geotextiles, and trench cap.
sections.applicability: Overview of collector-drain/drainage-layer construction placement.

sections.title: Design (Trench Geometry)
sections.summary: Trench width: 6 in clearance each side of the pipe; depth: >=12 in from subgrade surface to pipe center, plus 3 in clearance beneath the pipe; frost areas: place below frost penetration where practical (else top of pipe need not be deeper than 4 ft below the drainage-layer bottom); trench side slopes <=1V:10H (frost-affected pavements) or <=1V:4H (unpaved shoulder edge, not required in NFS/F1/S1 unless high-speed traffic); interior frost-area drains connect to the drainage layer via NFS fill + filter fabric only (not directly), with depth minimized for F3/F4 subgrades above the frost-penetration depth.
sections.body: In general the drainage layer is placed below the concrete surface in the case of rigid pavement and below the base course for a flexible pavement as illustrated in Figure C20-7, Figure C20-8, and Figure C20-9 (Appendix C). In most cases the trench for the collector drains should be constructed of sufficient width to provide 6 in (150 mm) clearance on each side of the pipe. The depth of the trench must be sufficient to provide a minimum 12 in (300 mm) from the top of the pavement subgrade to the center of the pipe plus 3 in (75 mm) clearance beneath the pipe. In frost areas extra care must be used in placing subsurface drains. For F3 and F4 subgrades a collector pipe will always be placed such that there will be positive drainage for the drainage layer and any NFS fill. If possible the drains should be placed below the depth of frost penetration. For many locations it will not be economically possible to place drains below the depth of frost penetration and therefore the drains and backfill will be subject to freezing. In areas where the depth of frost penetration is greater than 4 ft (1.2 m) below the bottom of the drainage layer, the top of the pipe need not be located deeper than 4 ft (1.2 m) below the bottom of the drainage layer. In frost areas where differential heave will cause pavement problems, the sides of the trench must be sloped not steeper than 1 vertical on 10 horizontal for the depth of frost penetration. At the edge of the pavement, where the pavement will not be subjected to traffic, the sides of the trench may be sloped at a slope of 1 vertical on 4 horizontal. The sloping of the trench sides is not required for the parts of the trench in NFS materials or for F1 or S1 soils unless the pavement over the trench is subjected to high speed traffic. The placement of collector drains under the interior portion of a pavement in frost areas is a special case where the collector drain is not directly connected to the drainage layer by an OGM or a RDM. This case is illustrated in Figure C20-7, Figure C20-8, and Figure C20-9 (Appendix C). The interior designs are based on the premise that NFS fill will have sufficient permeability to allow vertical drainage of the drainage layer into the collector pipes. Another premise is that the filter fabric will have sufficient area as not to impede the flow of water from the NFS fill to the collector pipe. The exception to the minimum requirement for the depth of the collector pipe below the surface of the subgrade is the interior case in a frost area for an F3 or F4 subgrade when the collection pipe is in above the depth of frost penetration. For this case the depth of the pipe below the surface of the subgrade is to be kept to a minimum.
key_points: Trench: 6 in clearance each side of pipe; depth >= 12 in (subgrade surface to pipe center) + 3 in clearance below pipe.
Frost-area trench side slopes: <= 1V:10H (differential-heave-critical areas) or <= 1V:4H (unpaved shoulder edge); not required in NFS/F1/S1 unless high-speed traffic.

sections.title: Backfill
sections.summary: Use permeable OGM/RDM/uniform-graded aggregate backfill; >=3 in beneath the pipe; compact/stabilize to prevent settlement, in <=6 in lifts; geocomposite backfill doesn't need high permeability (fabric is against the drained material) but does need to meet granular filter requirements against the trench side.
sections.body: Backfill the trench with a permeable material to rapidly convey water to the drainage pipe. The backfill material may be OGM, RDM, or other uniform graded aggregate. Place a minimum of 3 in (75 mm) of aggregate beneath the drainage pipe. Proper compaction or chemical stabilization of the backfill is necessary to prevent settlement of the fill. In placing the backfill, compact the backfill in lifts not exceeding 6 in (150 mm). When geocomposites are used in place of pipe, place the geocomposites against the material to be drained and thus the backfill is not expected to convey water. For this reason the backfill for the geocomposites will not require the high permeability required for the backfill around the pipe drains. However, since the backfill for the geocomposites will be against the side of the trench, the backfill should meet the requirements of a granular filter.
key_points: Use permeable OGM/RDM/uniform-graded aggregate backfill; >=3 in beneath the pipe; compact/stabilize to prevent settlement, in <=6 in lifts; geocomposite backfill doesn't need high permeability (fabric is against the drained material) but does need to meet granular filter...

sections.title: Geotextiles in the Trench
sections.summary: Nonwoven needle-punched filter fabric (Table 20-9) separates the trench backfill from subgrade/subbase and protects against surface-water-borne fines, without impeding flow from the drainage layer to the pipe.
sections.body: Provide the trench with a geotextile filter fabric. Place the filter fabric to separate the permeable backfill of the trench from the subgrade or subbase materials. The filter fabric must not be placed so as to impede the flow of water from the drainage layer to the drain pipe. The filter fabric must also protect from the infiltration of fines from any surface layer. This is particularly important for drains placed outside the pavement area where surface water can enter the drain through a soil surface. The filter fabric for the trench must be a nonwoven needle punched fabric meeting the criteria given in Table 20-9.
key_points: Nonwoven needle-punched filter fabric (Table 20-9) separates the trench backfill from subgrade/subbase and protects against surface-water-borne fines, without impeding flow from the drainage layer to the pipe.

sections.title: Trench Cap
sections.summary: Cap edge drains outside the paved area with a low-permeability layer (e.g. asphalt-stabilized surface) to limit surface-water infiltration; add a filter layer between the drain and sod if sod-surfaced.
sections.body: Cap edge drains placed outside of a paved area with a layer of low permeability material, such as an asphalt stabilized surface, to reduce the infiltration of surface water into the subsurface drainage system. If the area above the edge drain is to be sod surfaced, a filter layer will be required between the drain layer and sod.
key_points: Cap edge drains outside the paved area with a low-permeability layer (e.g. asphalt-stabilized surface) to limit surface-water infiltration; add a filter layer between the drain and sod if sod-surfaced.
sections.applicability: Capping edge drains outside the pavement.

sections.title: Lateral Outlet Pipe
sections.summary: See 20-5.4.1 (design) and 20-5.4.2 (outfall) for lateral outlet design and outfall protection.
sections.body: This section covers lateral outlet pipe design and outfall protection details.
key_points: See 20-5.4.1 (design) and 20-5.4.2 (outfall) for lateral outlet design and outfall protection.
sections.applicability: Overview of lateral outlet design.

sections.title: Design (Lateral Outlet)
sections.summary: Space lateral outlets 300-500 ft along edge drains and at all vertical-curve low points; ~45-degree angle from collector flow direction (cleanout ease); solid non-perforated pipe with an outlet structure; 3% slope to the outlet; invert >= 6 in above the 2-yr design ditch flow; low-permeability backfill or a cutoff wall/diaphragm around outlet pipe (anti-piping); dual outlets with large-radius bends aid flushing/maintenance; outlet pipe diameter matches the collector (or 4-6 in for geocomposite); frost areas need ice/snow-blockage protection for outlets.
sections.body: The lateral outlet pipe provides both a means of getting water out of the edge drains, and for cleaning and inspecting the system. Provide edge drains with lateral outlet pipes spaced at intervals 300 to 500 ft (90 to 150 m) along the edge drains and at the low point of all vertical curves. To facilitate drain cleanout, the outlet pipes should be placed at about a 45 degrees angle from the direction of flow in the collector drain. The lateral pipe should be a non-perforated solid-walled pipe and should be equipped with an outlet structure. A three percent slope from the edge drain to the outlet structure is recommended. To reduce outlet maintenance, outlet pipes should, where possible, be connected to existing storm drains or inlets. For lateral pipe flowing to a ditch, the invert of the outlet pipe should be a minimum of 6 in (150 mm) above the 2-year design flow in the ditch. To prevent piping, the trench for the outlet pipes must be backfilled with a material of low permeability, or provided with a cutoff wall or diaphragm. Dual outlets with large radius bend are recommended for maintenance considerations. The dual outlet system allows sections of collector drains to be flushed out to clear any debris material blocking the free flow of water. Other recommended design details for drainage outlets are as follows: for pipe drains, use the same diameter pipe as the collector drains (for prefabricated geocomposite drains, 4 in (100 mm) to 6 in (150 mm) diameter pipe should provide adequate hydraulic capacity); the discharge end of the outlet pipe should be placed at least 6 in (150 mm) above the 2 year design flow in the drainage ditch (same requirement applies even if discharging into storm drain inlets); in frost areas, give special attention to the placement of the outlet pipes such that they do not become clogged with ice or snow.
key_points: Lateral outlet spacing: 300-500 ft, plus at every vertical-curve low point.
Outlet invert: >= 6 in above the 2-year design ditch flow.

sections.title: Outfall for Outlet Pipe
sections.summary: Provide a headwall (precast or cast-in-place, flush with the slope for mowing) to protect the outlet, prevent erosion, and aid location; install easily-removed rodent screens.
sections.body: The outfall for the outlet pipe should be provided with a headwall to protect the outlet pipe from damage, prevent slope erosion, and facilitate the location of outlet pipes. Place headwalls flush with the slope so that mowing operations are not impaired. Easily removed rodent screens should be installed at the pipe outlet. The headwall may be pre-cast or cast-in-place.
key_points: Provide a headwall (precast or cast-in-place, flush with the slope for mowing) to protect the outlet, prevent erosion, and aid location; install easily-removed rodent screens.

sections.title: Reference Markers
sections.summary: Optional but recommended: mark outlets (flexible marker post or shoulder marking) for maintenance/observation.
sections.body: Although not a requirement, reference markers are recommended for the outlets to facilitate maintenance and observation. A simple flexible marker post or marking on the shoulder will suffice to mark the outlet.
key_points: Optional but recommended: mark outlets (flexible marker post or shoulder marking) for maintenance/observation.
sections.applicability: Optional outlet marking for maintenance.

sections.title: Cross Drains
sections.summary: Needed where flow is blocked, on steep grades to intercept water before drainage paths get too long, or at low points of vertical curves; typical locations: building-foundation abutments, bridge approach slabs, drainage-layer-to-impermeable-base transitions.
sections.body: Cross drains may be required at locations where flow in the drainage layer is blocked, on steep longitudinal grades where the water needs to be intercepted to prevent long drainage paths, or at the bottom of vertical curves. For example, cross drains may be required where pavements abut building foundations, at bridge approach slabs, or where drainage layers abut impermeable bases.
key_points: Needed where flow is blocked, on steep grades to intercept water before drainage paths get too long, or at low points of vertical curves; typical locations: building-foundation abutments, bridge approach slabs, drainage-layer-to-impermeable-base transitions.
sections.applicability: Identifying where cross drains are needed.

sections.title: Manholes and Observation
sections.summary: Manholes/observation basins/risers enable operation checks and pipe flushing/rodding; space manholes <=1,000 ft on subgrade pipe drains, with a flushing riser between manholes and at dead ends; manholes also at principal junctions.
sections.body: Manholes, observation basins, and risers are installed on subsurface drainage systems for access to the system to observe its operation and to flush or rod the pipe for cleaning. Manholes on subgrade pipe drains should be located at intervals of not over 1,000 ft (300 m) with one flushing riser located between manholes and at dead ends. Manholes should be provided at principal junction points of several drains.
key_points: Manhole spacing: <= 1,000 ft, plus a flushing riser between manholes and at dead ends.
sections.applicability: Manhole/riser spacing for maintenance access.
